days.title: Exam Strategy and an Overview of Ingestion Patterns

concepts.heading: Batch, Micro-Batch, and Streaming Ingestion
concepts.body: Data ingestion patterns fall on a spectrum from batch (large periodic loads, e.g. nightly S3 uploads or Glue jobs) to micro-batch (small frequent batches, seconds to minutes) to true streaming (continuous, sub-second to low-second processing with Kinesis or MSK). The right choice depends on latency requirements, cost tolerance, and downstream consumer needs: streaming infrastructure runs continuously and costs more to operate, while batch is cheaper but introduces latency. On the exam, look for latency clues ('real-time', 'within seconds', 'nightly') to identify which pattern -- and therefore which service family -- is being tested.

concepts.heading: AWS DMS: Database Migration and CDC
concepts.body: AWS Database Migration Service replicates data between heterogeneous or homogeneous database engines, supporting a Full Load (one-time snapshot copy) and Full Load plus CDC (Change Data Capture), which continues to stream ongoing inserts, updates, and deletes after the initial load completes. DMS reads the source database's transaction/redo logs rather than querying tables directly, which keeps the load on the source database minimal. It is the standard answer whenever a scenario needs to migrate an on-premises or EC2-hosted database to RDS/Aurora with near-zero downtime, or to continuously replicate an operational database into a data lake for analytics. A common gotcha: DMS does not perform schema conversion between different engines -- for that, you pair it with the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT).

concepts.heading: AWS AppFlow for SaaS Integration
concepts.body: AppFlow is a no-code integration service that moves data between AWS services and SaaS applications such as Salesforce, ServiceNow, SAP, and Zendesk, without writing custom API integration code. Flows can run on a schedule, on-demand, or be triggered by events in the source application, and AppFlow supports built-in data transformations like field mapping, filtering, and validation during transfer. It is the go-to answer when a question mentions ingesting from a named SaaS platform, since building and maintaining custom API connectors for these platforms is exactly what AppFlow eliminates. Note that AppFlow is not meant for arbitrary REST APIs -- it only supports a defined list of connectors.

concepts.heading: AWS Transfer Family for File-Based Ingestion
concepts.body: Transfer Family provides fully managed SFTP, FTPS, and FTP endpoints backed by S3 or EFS, letting external partners and legacy systems push and pull files using protocols they already use, without you operating your own FTP servers. It integrates with IAM and Lambda for custom authentication (including Active Directory) and can trigger downstream processing automatically when a file lands. This is the answer whenever a scenario explicitly requires legacy file-transfer protocol compatibility for external partners, as opposed to a native AWS API-based ingestion path.

concepts.heading: Picking the Right Ingestion Service
concepts.body: A fast decision framework for Domain 1 questions: if the scenario says 'real-time' or 'seconds of latency', think Kinesis Data Streams or MSK; if it says 'database migration' or 'ongoing replication from an RDS/on-prem DB', think DMS; if it names a SaaS application, think AppFlow; and if it mentions SFTP/FTPS or external partner file drops, think Transfer Family. Misreading these keywords is one of the most common sources of wrong answers on this exam, so practice scanning questions specifically for the ingestion-pattern and source-system clues before evaluating the answer choices.

examPoints: When a question emphasizes 'real-time' or a latency measured in seconds, batch-oriented services like Glue batch jobs or EMR batch clusters are almost always the wrong answer -- favor Kinesis or MSK instead.

A scenario describing an on-premises database that must move to AWS with minimal downtime and continued replication during a cutover window is the classic DMS Full Load + CDC pattern -- memorize that pairing.

quiz.q: A company needs to ingest clickstream data from its website with end-to-end latency measured in single-digit seconds so a fraud-detection application can react immediately. Which service should the data engineer choose?
choices: AWS Glue batch job scheduled hourly
Amazon S3 with daily batch uploads
quiz.explain: Kinesis Data Streams is purpose-built for continuous, low-latency streaming ingestion; the other options are all batch-oriented and would introduce minutes-to-hours of delay.

quiz.q: An organization is migrating an on-premises Oracle database to Amazon Aurora and must keep the two databases synchronized during a multi-week cutover period, capturing every insert, update, and delete made to the source in the meantime. What should the engineer configure?
choices: An AWS Glue Crawler on a nightly schedule
AWS DMS with Full Load plus CDC replication
Amazon Data Firehose writing to Aurora
AWS Snowball Edge for a one-time transfer
quiz.explain: DMS Full Load + CDC performs the initial bulk copy and then continuously streams ongoing changes from the source transaction logs; Snowball Edge (closed to new customers since 2025-11-07) only handles a one-time transfer and cannot capture ongoing changes.

days.recap: Ingestion patterns range from batch to streaming based on latency needs; DMS handles database migration plus CDC replication, AppFlow handles SaaS integration, and Transfer Family handles managed SFTP/FTPS file exchange.

days.title: Kinesis Data Streams: Shards, Throughput, and Fan-Out

concepts.heading: Shards as the Unit of Throughput
concepts.body: A Kinesis Data Streams shard is the fundamental unit of capacity: each shard supports up to 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s of writes, and up to 2 MB/s of reads (shared across standard consumers). Stream throughput scales linearly by adding shards, so a workload that needs 5 MB/s of ingest requires at least five shards. Exceeding a shard's write throughput returns a ProvisionedThroughputExceededException, which producers must handle with retry and backoff logic rather than treating as a fatal error.

concepts.heading: Partition Keys and Hot Shards
concepts.body: Every record is assigned to a shard based on a hash of its partition key, so records sharing a key always land on the same shard, preserving per-key ordering. If a small number of keys receive disproportionate traffic, a 'hot shard' results, where that shard throttles while others sit idle even though overall stream capacity is sufficient. Simply adding more shards does not fix this, because the same skewed keys keep hashing to the same shard; the real fix is choosing a higher-cardinality, more evenly distributed partition key, sometimes with a random suffix (salting) added to hot keys.

concepts.heading: On-Demand vs. Provisioned Capacity Mode
concepts.body: On-Demand mode automatically scales shard count based on observed throughput over the past 30 days, with no capacity planning required, at a higher per-unit cost. Provisioned mode requires you to explicitly manage shard count and perform resharding (splitting or merging shards) as traffic changes, which is cheaper at steady, predictable volumes but requires operational attention. Exam scenarios describing unpredictable or spiky traffic with minimal operational overhead point to On-Demand; steady, well-understood throughput favors Provisioned for cost efficiency.

concepts.heading: Enhanced Fan-Out for Low-Latency Multi-Consumer Reads
concepts.body: By default, all consumers of a shard share that shard's 2 MB/s read throughput via polling (GetRecords), so latency grows as more consumers are added. Enhanced Fan-Out (EFO) gives each registered consumer its own dedicated 2 MB/s pipe per shard, pushed over HTTP/2 rather than polled, delivering consistently low latency (typically under 70ms) even with many parallel consumers. EFO costs more per consumer-shard-hour, so it is used specifically when multiple independent applications must read the same stream with low latency simultaneously -- a single-consumer pipeline rarely needs it.

examPoints: A requirement for multiple independent consumer applications to read the same stream simultaneously with minimal latency is the signature clue for Enhanced Fan-Out -- plain shared-throughput consumers would slow down as more readers are added.

Repeated ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors concentrated on a subset of shards point to a partition-key design problem, not a capacity problem -- the fix is a better key, not simply more shards.

quiz.q: Several independent consumer applications must all read from the same Kinesis Data Streams stream with the lowest possible latency, and adding more consumers should not degrade performance for existing ones. What should the data engineer implement?
quiz.explain: Enhanced Fan-Out gives each consumer a dedicated 2 MB/s throughput pipe per shard, so adding consumers doesn't degrade others; more shards wouldn't fix shared read throughput contention among existing consumers.

quiz.q: A stream is repeatedly throttling on one specific shard while the rest of the shards are nearly idle, even though total account throughput is well under the stream's overall capacity. What is the most effective long-term fix?
choices: Redesign the partition key to distribute traffic more evenly
quiz.explain: A hot shard is a partition-key distribution problem; records with the same key always map to the same shard, so adding shards without changing the key does not relieve the imbalance.

days.recap: Shards define throughput (1 MB/s write, 2 MB/s read); hot shards are fixed by redesigning the partition key, not by adding shards; and Enhanced Fan-Out gives each consumer dedicated low-latency throughput.

days.title: Amazon Data Firehose and Managed Service for Apache Flink

concepts.heading: Firehose as a Fully Managed Delivery Service
concepts.body: Amazon Data Firehose is a serverless delivery pipeline that automatically buffers incoming records and delivers them to destinations such as S3, Redshift, OpenSearch Service, and HTTP endpoints, without you provisioning or managing shards or a consumer application. Because it is purely a delivery mechanism, Firehose is the right answer whenever a scenario needs streaming data landed reliably in a destination with no custom consumer logic; if custom real-time processing is required, Kinesis Data Streams with your own consumer is the better fit.

concepts.heading: Buffering, Batching, and Minimum Latency
concepts.body: Firehose batches records based on a buffer size (in MB) or a buffer interval (in seconds), delivering whenever whichever threshold is reached first, which means there is an inherent minimum latency of roughly 60 seconds even at the lowest buffer interval setting. This buffering is what allows Firehose to write efficiently sized objects to S3 rather than many tiny files, which also helps downstream query performance. A common exam trap is expecting Firehose to deliver in true sub-second real time -- it cannot, because buffering is fundamental to how it operates.

concepts.heading: In-Flight Transformation with Lambda
concepts.body: Firehose can invoke a Lambda function to transform, enrich, or filter each record before delivery, and it also supports built-in format conversion (e.g., JSON to Parquet or ORC) so data lands in an analytics-friendly columnar format without a separate ETL step. This built-in conversion is a common reason to choose Firehose over hand-rolled delivery when the destination is a data lake that will be queried with Athena or Redshift Spectrum.

concepts.heading: Managed Service for Apache Flink for Real-Time Analytics
concepts.body: Managed Service for Apache Flink (formerly Kinesis Data Analytics) runs streaming SQL, Java, or Python applications directly against a Kinesis or MSK stream, supporting windowed aggregations (tumbling, sliding, and session windows) for use cases like real-time dashboards, anomaly detection, and rolling metrics. Unlike Firehose, which only delivers data, Flink actually computes over the stream in near real time before results are emitted onward. Choose it whenever a scenario requires continuous SQL-style aggregation or stateful stream processing, not just delivery.

examPoints: A requirement described as 'serverless', 'no infrastructure to manage', and 'load streaming data into S3 or Redshift' is Firehose's signature phrasing; a requirement for custom consumer logic points back to Kinesis Data Streams instead.

When a scenario needs a running SQL aggregation, sliding window, or real-time anomaly score computed directly on the stream, that is Managed Service for Apache Flink, not Firehose, which cannot perform stateful computation.

quiz.q: A company wants to land streaming clickstream events into S3 in Parquet format without operating any consumer infrastructure. Which service satisfies this with the least operational overhead?
choices: Kinesis Data Streams with a custom Lambda consumer
Amazon Data Firehose with format conversion enabled
Amazon MSK with a Kafka Connect S3 sink
quiz.explain: Firehose is fully managed and includes built-in JSON-to-Parquet conversion during delivery, requiring no custom consumer code, unlike the Kinesis Data Streams option.

quiz.q: An analytics team needs to compute a rolling 5-minute average of sensor readings directly from a live stream and continuously emit the result. What should be used?
choices: Managed Service for Apache Flink with a tumbling window
quiz.explain: Flink-based stream processing natively supports windowed aggregations over live data; Athena and Redshift Spectrum query data at rest, not continuously streaming records.

days.recap: Firehose is serverless buffered delivery to destinations like S3/Redshift with optional format conversion, while Managed Service for Apache Flink performs real-time SQL-based windowed computation directly on the stream.

days.title: Amazon MSK: When Kafka Compatibility Matters

concepts.heading: MSK vs. Kinesis: The Core Decision Point
concepts.body: Amazon MSK is a managed Apache Kafka service that is fully API-compatible with open-source Kafka, meaning existing Kafka producers, consumers, consumer groups, and exactly-once processing semantics continue to work unmodified. Kinesis Data Streams uses its own proprietary API and SDKs. The single most important exam signal for choosing between them is whether the scenario mentions existing Kafka client code, Kafka Connect ecosystem tooling, or a need to preserve open-source Kafka compatibility -- if so, MSK is correct even though Kinesis might otherwise seem like the 'AWS-native' answer.

concepts.heading: MSK Serverless for Unpredictable Workloads
concepts.body: MSK Serverless automatically provisions and scales broker capacity and storage based on incoming traffic, removing the need to plan broker count, instance size, or storage ahead of time. It is best suited to workloads with unpredictable or spiky throughput where a provisioned Kafka cluster would otherwise be sized for peak and sit under-utilized most of the time; it does have some throughput ceilings and fewer configuration knobs than provisioned MSK.

concepts.heading: MSK Connect for Managed Kafka Connectors
concepts.body: MSK Connect runs Kafka Connect source and sink connectors (for example, an S3 sink connector or a Debezium CDC source connector) as a managed service, handling scaling and fault tolerance for the connector workers without you operating your own Kafka Connect cluster on EC2. This is the answer whenever a scenario needs to move data into or out of an MSK topic using standard Kafka Connect connectors without managing the connector infrastructure directly.

concepts.heading: Topic Design and Partition Count
concepts.body: An MSK topic's partition count determines its maximum parallelism, since each partition can only be actively read by one consumer within a given consumer group at a time -- too few partitions caps throughput and limits how many consumer instances can usefully run in parallel, while too many partitions increases broker overhead and rebalance time. Unlike Kinesis shards, Kafka partitions are not typically resized as fluidly, so getting an appropriate partition count early, based on expected peak consumer parallelism, avoids a disruptive later migration to a new topic.

examPoints: A scenario describing an existing on-premises Kafka application, existing consumer group logic, or a need for Kafka Connect connectors is a strong MSK signal, since Kinesis is not Kafka-API compatible and cannot run that code unmodified.

When traffic patterns are unpredictable and the team does not want to plan broker capacity ahead of time, MSK Serverless removes the sizing decision entirely, similar in spirit to Kinesis On-Demand mode.

quiz.q: A team is migrating an existing on-premises Kafka-based pipeline to AWS and wants to reuse its existing Kafka consumer group code without modification. Which service should they choose?
quiz.explain: MSK is fully compatible with the open-source Kafka API, so existing consumer group code runs unchanged; Kinesis uses a different, proprietary API and would require a rewrite.

quiz.q: A workload has highly unpredictable and bursty throughput, and the team does not want to forecast or manage broker capacity for its Kafka cluster. What should they use?
choices: MSK Standard with a fixed broker count
quiz.explain: MSK Serverless automatically scales brokers and storage with traffic, eliminating capacity planning, whereas MSK Standard requires you to size and manage brokers yourself.

days.recap: MSK is the answer whenever Kafka-API compatibility or existing Kafka tooling matters; MSK Serverless removes capacity planning for unpredictable traffic; and MSK Connect runs managed Kafka Connect connectors.

days.title: AWS Glue Fundamentals: The Data Catalog and Crawlers

concepts.heading: The Glue Data Catalog as Shared Metadata
concepts.body: The Glue Data Catalog is a central, persistent metadata store that holds table definitions -- schema, location, partitioning, and format -- which Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR, and Glue Jobs all read from as a common source of truth. Because multiple engines share the same catalog, a table cataloged once can immediately be queried by Athena and also processed by a Glue Spark job without redefining its schema in each tool. This shared-catalog design is what enables a true 'lake house' pattern across services.

concepts.heading: Crawlers: Automated Schema Discovery
concepts.body: A Glue Crawler connects to a data store (S3, JDBC, DynamoDB, etc.), samples the underlying files or tables, infers the schema using built-in or custom classifiers, and then creates or updates a table definition in the Data Catalog automatically. This removes the need to hand-write DDL for evolving or unknown datasets, but it is not free to run repeatedly at scale -- a crawler re-scanning millions of S3 objects on every run can become slow and costly, which is why scheduling and incremental crawling matter in production.

concepts.heading: Glue Job Types: Spark, Python Shell, and Ray
concepts.body: Glue Spark jobs run distributed transformations across a managed Spark cluster and are the right choice for large-scale, parallelizable ETL. Python Shell jobs run a single Python script without spinning up a Spark cluster, making them far cheaper and faster to start for small scripts, lightweight API calls, or non-Spark Python libraries. Glue jobs with Ray support scaling out Python-native (often ML-oriented) workloads across a Ray cluster (closed to new customers since 2026-04-30; AWS points new Ray workloads to Amazon EKS with KubeRay). Choosing the wrong job type for the data volume is a frequent real-world and exam mistake -- using Spark for a handful of megabytes wastes cluster startup time and cost.

concepts.heading: Glue Studio's Visual ETL Interface
concepts.body: Glue Studio lets you build ETL jobs visually by connecting source, transform, and target nodes on a canvas, automatically generating the underlying Spark (DynamicFrame-based) code. It's aimed at engineers who want to compose common transformations (joins, filters, format conversions) quickly without writing Spark code from scratch, while still allowing custom code nodes for logic the visual editor doesn't cover.

examPoints: A requirement to automatically detect the schema of new files landing in S3 without manually writing table DDL is the textbook Crawler use case.

When the workload is a small script processing a few megabytes with a non-Spark library, a Python Shell job is both cheaper and faster to start than a full Spark job -- picking Spark here is a common wrong answer.

quiz.q: A data engineer wants Data Catalog tables to be created and kept up to date automatically as new files with a consistent schema land in an S3 bucket, without manually writing table definitions. What should they configure?
quiz.explain: A Crawler scans the data store, infers its schema, and creates or updates the corresponding Data Catalog table automatically; the other options don't perform schema discovery.

quiz.q: A small transformation script processes a few megabytes of data using a lightweight Python library and needs to run as cheaply and quickly as possible. Which Glue job type is the best fit?
quiz.explain: A Python Shell job runs without provisioning a Spark cluster, making it far cheaper and faster to start for small, non-distributed workloads than a Spark job.

days.recap: The Data Catalog is the shared metadata layer across Athena/Redshift Spectrum/EMR/Glue; Crawlers automate schema discovery; and Glue job type (Spark vs. Python Shell vs. Ray) should match data volume and workload shape.

days.title: AWS Glue in Depth: Job Bookmarks, DPUs, and DataBrew

concepts.heading: Job Bookmarks for Incremental Processing
concepts.body: Job bookmarks track which source data (files, partitions, or JDBC rows by primary key) a Glue job has already processed across runs, so a scheduled job reprocesses only new data instead of the entire dataset every time. Bookmarks must be explicitly enabled and rely on the job being written to use them consistently (e.g., not overwriting the same source paths); disabling and re-enabling a bookmark, or resetting it, is the standard technique when you deliberately need to reprocess historical data.

concepts.heading: DPUs and Worker Scaling
concepts.body: A Data Processing Unit (DPU) represents a unit of compute (4 vCPU and 16 GB memory equivalent) that Glue jobs consume, and job capacity is configured through a Worker Type (G.1X, G.2X, or G.025X) combined with a number of workers, which together determine parallelism and memory available for each Spark executor. When a job fails with out-of-memory errors on large joins or skewed data, increasing the worker type/count or reducing data skew (e.g., via repartitioning) are the standard remediation paths, in that order of investigation.

concepts.heading: DynamicFrame vs. Spark DataFrame
concepts.body: A DynamicFrame is Glue's own data abstraction, similar to a Spark DataFrame but designed to tolerate inconsistent or evolving schemas within the same dataset -- for example, a column that is sometimes an integer and sometimes a string across different files. The resolveChoice() transform explicitly resolves such type ambiguities (by casting, keeping one type, or splitting into separate columns) before further processing. This flexibility makes DynamicFrames well suited to messy, semi-structured source data, though you can convert to and from a native Spark DataFrame when you need Spark-specific operations.

concepts.heading: Glue DataBrew for No-Code Data Preparation
concepts.body: Glue DataBrew provides a visual, no-code interface with over 250 pre-built transformations for cleaning, normalizing, and profiling data -- useful for analysts who need to explore data quality (missing values, outliers, distributions) and build repeatable cleaning 'recipes' without writing Spark or Python code. DataBrew is about interactive data preparation and profiling, distinct from Glue Data Quality, which enforces declarative pass/fail rules in a pipeline.

examPoints: A requirement that a daily job must not reprocess files it already handled on previous runs is the standard signal for enabling Job Bookmarks.
A Glue Spark job failing with out-of-memory errors on a large join should first be diagnosed for data skew and worker sizing before assuming more workers alone will fix it.

quiz.q: A Glue job runs nightly against an S3 prefix that receives new files daily, and it must avoid reprocessing files it already handled on prior runs. What feature should be enabled?
quiz.explain: Job Bookmarks track previously processed data across runs so only new data is processed; the other options do not address incremental processing.

quiz.q: A business analyst wants to visually clean and profile a dataset -- checking for missing values and outliers -- without writing any code. Which service fits this need?
quiz.explain: DataBrew offers a no-code visual interface with built-in profiling and cleaning transformations aimed at exactly this kind of analyst workflow.

days.recap: Job Bookmarks enable incremental processing, DPUs/Worker Type control job scale and are the first lever for OOM failures, DynamicFrames tolerate schema inconsistency, and DataBrew offers no-code visual data prep.

days.title: Orchestration: Step Functions vs. MWAA

concepts.heading: Step Functions for Serverless AWS-Native Workflows
concepts.body: AWS Step Functions coordinates multiple AWS services (Lambda, Glue, ECS, SNS, etc.) as a serverless state machine, with built-in retry, catch, and error-handling logic defined declaratively, and a visual Workflow Studio for designing the flow. It is well suited to workflows composed primarily of AWS-native service calls with conditional branching, and it scales automatically with no infrastructure to manage. Because retries and error branches are first-class constructs, Step Functions handles transient failures more gracefully than a hand-rolled script would.

concepts.heading: Amazon MWAA for Existing Airflow Investments
concepts.body: Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (MWAA) runs a managed Apache Airflow environment, letting teams reuse existing DAGs, custom operators, and the broader Airflow plugin ecosystem rather than rewriting orchestration logic for AWS-native tools. It is the right choice whenever an organization already has substantial Airflow investment or needs Airflow-specific features (like complex cross-DAG dependencies) that don't map cleanly onto a state machine model. MWAA carries more operational overhead and cost than Step Functions for simple workflows, since it runs a persistent environment rather than being purely event-driven.

concepts.heading: EventBridge Scheduler for Simple Time-Based Triggers
concepts.body: EventBridge Scheduler triggers targets on a cron or rate-based schedule with no dependency management between steps -- it is meant for simple, independent, recurring invocations (e.g., 'run this Lambda every night at 2 AM') rather than for coordinating multi-step workflows with branching logic. When a scenario needs only a simple recurring trigger and nothing else, reaching for Step Functions or MWAA would be over-engineering.

concepts.heading: Glue Workflows for Glue-Only Pipelines
concepts.body: Glue Workflows orchestrate a pipeline composed entirely of Glue resources -- crawlers, jobs, and triggers -- within the Glue console itself, tracking dependencies between them (e.g., 'run this job only after that crawler completes'). It is a narrower tool than Step Functions, useful specifically when the entire pipeline lives inside Glue and doesn't need to coordinate with services outside the Glue ecosystem.

examPoints: A scenario describing existing Airflow DAGs, custom operators, or hundreds of complex interdependent tasks that must be preserved points to MWAA rather than rebuilding the workflow in Step Functions.

A workflow connecting several native AWS services with conditional branches, where 'serverless' and minimal operational overhead are emphasized, points to Step Functions over MWAA or a fixed EventBridge schedule.

quiz.q: A pipeline needs to invoke several Glue jobs, a Lambda function, and an SNS notification with conditional branching based on job success or failure, using only AWS-native services with no persistent infrastructure to manage. What should be used?
quiz.explain: Step Functions serverlessly orchestrates AWS service calls with native retry/catch and conditional branching; Glue Workflows can't coordinate Lambda and SNS, and EventBridge Scheduler has no branching logic.

quiz.q: A team wants to lift-and-shift a complex set of existing Apache Airflow DAGs, including several custom operators, into AWS with minimal rewriting. What is the best option?
quiz.explain: MWAA runs a managed Airflow environment, allowing existing DAGs and custom operators to be reused largely as-is, unlike Step Functions which would require rewriting the workflow as a state machine.

days.recap: Step Functions is serverless AWS-native orchestration with built-in retry/catch, MWAA preserves existing Airflow assets, EventBridge Scheduler handles simple recurring triggers, and Glue Workflows orchestrate Glue-only pipelines.

days.title: File Formats, Partitioning, CDC, and Idempotency

concepts.heading: Columnar Formats: Parquet and ORC
concepts.body: Parquet and ORC store data column-by-column rather than row-by-row, which lets query engines like Athena and Redshift Spectrum read only the columns referenced by a query (column pruning) and apply more effective compression since values within a column tend to be similar. This typically reduces both bytes scanned (lowering cost, since Athena charges per TB scanned) and query time compared to row-based formats like CSV or JSON, especially for wide tables with selective queries. Converting raw ingested data to Parquet is one of the most common and highest-leverage optimizations in a data lake.

concepts.heading: S3 Partitioning for Query Pruning
concepts.body: Hive-style partitioning (e.g., s3://bucket/table/year=2025/month=01/day=15/) organizes objects into a directory structure that lets query engines skip entire partitions that don't match a query's filter, dramatically reducing scanned data for time-filtered queries. Partitioning should align with how the data is actually filtered -- most commonly by date -- and its granularity should be tuned to data volume, since a mismatch causes either too many small files or partitions that are still too large to prune effectively.

concepts.heading: The Small File Problem from Over-Partitioning
concepts.body: Partitioning too finely (for example, by hour or minute for a low-volume dataset) produces a very large number of small objects, which increases metadata overhead in the Data Catalog, slows crawlers, and forces query engines to open many small files instead of a few well-sized ones -- often making queries slower despite partitioning being 'more granular.' The fix typically involves choosing coarser partition boundaries and periodically compacting small files into fewer, larger ones (for example, via a Glue job or CTAS in Athena).

concepts.heading: Change Data Capture (CDC) Patterns
concepts.body: CDC captures only the rows that changed in a source system (inserts, updates, deletes) rather than re-extracting the entire dataset on every run, dramatically reducing latency and cost compared to full reloads for large, slowly-changing tables. DMS is the most common AWS CDC mechanism for relational databases, reading from transaction logs, while DynamoDB Streams and Debezium-on-MSK serve similar roles for other sources. Applying CDC changes downstream correctly (especially deletes and out-of-order updates) requires careful handling in the target, which is a frequent source of pipeline bugs.

concepts.heading: Idempotency in Pipeline Design
concepts.body: An idempotent operation produces the same end state no matter how many times it is executed with the same input, which is essential for safe retries after a partial failure -- without it, retrying a failed job could double-count records or corrupt downstream state. Common techniques include using deterministic object keys, upserts (MERGE) instead of blind inserts, and Job Bookmarks or explicit watermarking to avoid reprocessing the same source data twice. Idempotency should be treated as a design requirement from the start, not an afterthought bolted on after a production incident.

examPoints: When a question asks how to simultaneously reduce Athena query cost and improve query speed, the standard combined answer is converting to a columnar format like Parquet and partitioning by a commonly filtered column such as date.
A scenario where over-fine partitioning made queries slower rather than faster describes the small file problem -- the fix is coarser partitions and periodic compaction, not simply more partitioning.

quiz.q: A team wants to reduce both the cost and runtime of frequent Athena queries against a large dataset. What combination is most effective?
choices: XML format stored as a single large file
quiz.explain: Columnar Parquet enables column pruning and better compression, while date-based partitioning lets Athena skip irrelevant partitions entirely -- together they minimize bytes scanned.

quiz.q: After partitioning a table by hour instead of by day, query performance actually got worse. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The small file problem, caused by excessive partition granularity
quiz.explain: Overly fine partitioning creates many small objects, increasing metadata and I/O overhead; the fix is coarser partitioning and file compaction, not finer partitioning.

days.recap: Parquet plus sensible date-based partitioning is the standard combo for cheaper, faster queries; over-partitioning causes the small file problem; and CDC plus idempotent pipeline design keep incremental processing correct.

days.title: Domain 1 Review: Data Ingestion and Transformation

concepts.heading: The Domain 1 Service Map
concepts.body: Domain 1 covers everything from getting data into AWS to transforming it into an analytics-ready shape: DMS and AppFlow handle batch and SaaS ingestion respectively, Kinesis Data Streams and MSK handle real-time streaming (native AWS API vs. Kafka-compatible), Firehose and Managed Service for Apache Flink handle streaming delivery and computation, and Glue covers the bulk of batch ETL, cataloging, and orchestration. Being able to place any given service correctly into this map, rather than memorizing services in isolation, is what separates a strong Domain 1 score from a shaky one.

concepts.heading: A Decision Tree for Service Selection
concepts.body: A reliable mental decision tree: if the requirement is real-time with an AWS-native API, choose Kinesis; if it is real-time but must be Kafka-API compatible, choose MSK; if it is a scheduled batch ETL transformation, choose Glue; and if it is a one-time or ongoing database migration, choose DMS. Practicing applying this tree quickly, before reading the answer choices in detail, prevents getting anchored on a plausible-sounding wrong answer.

concepts.heading: Recurring Head-to-Head Comparisons
concepts.body: The exam frequently tests near-identical-sounding pairs: Kinesis Data Streams (custom consumer, low-latency, complex logic) versus Firehose (fully managed delivery, no custom consumer); MSK (Kafka-compatible) versus Kinesis (AWS-native API); and Glue Spark jobs (large-scale distributed) versus Python Shell jobs (lightweight scripts). Reviewing these as explicit pairs, rather than each service independently, closes most of the remaining gaps before moving to Domain 2.

concepts.heading: Format and Pipeline Hygiene
concepts.body: Underneath the service-selection questions, Domain 1 also tests pipeline hygiene: columnar formats and sensible partitioning for cost/performance, CDC for efficient incremental capture, and idempotent job design for safe retries. These cross-cutting concepts show up embedded inside scenario questions about specific services, so they are worth reviewing on their own rather than assuming they were 'covered' inside a single day's material.

examPoints: Domain 1 carries the largest exam weight at 34%, so any service you're still unsure about after this review deserves a dedicated re-read of its original day before moving on.

Build the habit of underlining latency, compatibility, and infrastructure-management keywords ('real-time', 'existing Kafka', 'serverless', 'no infrastructure to manage') in every scenario question, since they are usually the deciding factor between similar-looking answer choices.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a fully managed, Kafka-API-compatible streaming service on AWS?
quiz.explain: MSK is Kafka-API compatible; Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose use AWS-native APIs instead.

quiz.q: Which Glue feature prevents a recurring job from reprocessing files it has already handled on a previous run?
quiz.explain: Job Bookmarks track already-processed source data across runs to enable incremental processing.

days.recap: Domain 1 review complete: if you can explain, from memory, why each service in this week was chosen over its closest alternative, you're ready to move to Domain 2.

days.title: S3 Storage Classes, Lifecycle Policies, and Apache Iceberg

concepts.heading: The S3 Storage Class Spectrum
concepts.body: S3 offers a range of storage classes trading cost against retrieval latency and availability: Standard for frequently accessed data, Standard-IA and One Zone-IA for infrequent access at lower storage cost but with a retrieval fee, and the Glacier tiers (Instant Retrieval, Flexible Retrieval, and Deep Archive) for archival data with retrieval times ranging from milliseconds to many hours. Choosing the wrong class for an access pattern either wastes money (storing rarely-read data in Standard) or introduces unacceptable retrieval latency (archiving data that's actually accessed regularly).

concepts.heading: Intelligent-Tiering for Unpredictable Access Patterns
concepts.body: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically monitors each object's access pattern and moves it between frequent-access and infrequent-access tiers (and optionally archive tiers) without operational effort or retrieval fees for the standard tiers, in exchange for a small monthly monitoring fee per object. It is specifically the right answer when a scenario says access patterns are unknown or unpredictable, since manually chosen static storage classes could easily be wrong in either direction for such data.

concepts.heading: Lifecycle Policies for Automated Data Retention
concepts.body: S3 Lifecycle rules automatically transition objects between storage classes or expire (delete) them after a specified number of days, letting you encode a data retention policy (e.g., 'move to IA after 30 days, Glacier after 90, delete after 7 years') declaratively rather than through manual or scripted cleanup. Lifecycle rules apply per prefix or tag, so different retention policies can coexist within the same bucket for different datasets.

concepts.heading: Apache Iceberg and S3 Tables for Lakehouse Semantics
concepts.body: Apache Iceberg is an open table format that adds database-like features on top of files stored in S3 -- ACID transactions across concurrent writers, schema evolution without rewriting existing data, and time travel to query a table as of a past snapshot -- capabilities that plain S3 objects with a Hive-style catalog do not provide. S3 Tables is AWS's native, managed implementation of Iceberg tables directly on S3, handling maintenance operations like compaction automatically. Whenever a scenario mentions ACID guarantees, concurrent writers, schema evolution, or time travel on a data lake, Iceberg/S3 Tables is the intended answer rather than a plain Parquet-on-S3 table.

examPoints: A scenario that explicitly says access patterns cannot be predicted in advance is the signature phrase for Intelligent-Tiering rather than manually selecting a fixed storage class.
Keywords like 'ACID transactions', 'schema evolution', or 'time travel' on data lake tables point specifically to Apache Iceberg / S3 Tables, not a plain S3 + Glue Catalog setup.

quiz.q: A dataset has highly unpredictable access patterns, and the team wants storage costs automatically optimized without manual tier management. What should they use?
choices: S3 Glacier Deep Archive for everything
quiz.explain: Intelligent-Tiering automatically monitors access patterns and moves objects between tiers, which is exactly suited to unpredictable access, unlike any single fixed storage class.

quiz.q: A data lake table needs ACID transaction guarantees, schema evolution support, and the ability to query prior snapshots of the data. What should the engineer use?
quiz.explain: Iceberg provides ACID transactions, schema evolution, and time travel on top of S3 data, none of which plain files or storage classes alone provide.

days.recap: S3 storage classes trade cost against retrieval speed based on access frequency, Intelligent-Tiering automates that trade-off for unpredictable patterns, Lifecycle rules automate retention, and Iceberg/S3 Tables add ACID and time-travel semantics to the lake.

days.title: Data Lake Governance with AWS Lake Formation

concepts.heading: Lake Formation's Central Permission Model
concepts.body: Lake Formation centralizes data lake access control at a finer grain than IAM alone can provide, supporting table-, column-, and row-level permissions layered on top of the underlying S3 and Glue Catalog resources. Rather than managing S3 bucket policies and IAM policies per consumer, administrators grant permissions in Lake Formation once, and it enforces them consistently across Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR, and other integrated engines.

concepts.heading: LF-Tags for Scalable, Attribute-Based Access Control
concepts.body: LF-Tags let administrators attach key-value tags to databases, tables, or columns, and then grant permissions based on tag values rather than naming every individual resource -- for example, granting access to everything tagged classification=public without listing each table. This scales far better than resource-by-resource grants in large organizations with hundreds or thousands of tables, since new tables that inherit the right tags automatically pick up the correct permissions.

concepts.heading: Blueprints for Automated Ingestion Workflows
concepts.body: Lake Formation Blueprints generate pre-built workflows (Glue jobs, crawlers, and triggers) for common ingestion patterns, such as an initial bulk load plus incremental loads from a relational database into the lake, reducing the manual setup needed to bootstrap a new source into the governed lake. A Blueprint asks for the source connection, target database, and schedule, then provisions the underlying Glue resources automatically, which is significantly faster than hand-building an equivalent crawler-plus-job pipeline for a routine, well-understood ingestion pattern.

concepts.heading: Row- and Column-Level Data Filters
concepts.body: Lake Formation data filters let administrators restrict specific rows (for example, only rows for a given region) or specific columns (for example, hiding a salary column) that a given principal can see, all enforced at query time by the integrated engines rather than requiring separate physically filtered copies of the data. This is the mechanism to reach for whenever a requirement calls for different user groups to see different subsets of the same underlying table.

examPoints: A requirement to grant the same access policy across hundreds of tables without listing each one individually is the classic LF-Tags use case, versus per-resource IAM or Lake Formation grants which don't scale as well.

Hiding a specific sensitive column (like salary or SSN) from one group while allowing full access to another group on the same table is a Lake Formation column-level data filter, not an S3 bucket policy, which cannot see inside object contents at that granularity.

quiz.q: An organization wants to manage access to hundreds of Glue Catalog tables without granting permissions to each table individually. What Lake Formation feature should they use?
quiz.explain: LF-Tags let you grant access based on attribute tags applied to resources, scaling to large numbers of tables without per-resource grants.

quiz.q: A specific department should not be able to see a salary column in an otherwise shared table. What should be configured?
choices: A Lake Formation column-level permission/data filter
quiz.explain: Lake Formation supports fine-grained column- and row-level access control enforced at query time, which S3 bucket policies cannot express.

days.recap: Lake Formation layers fine-grained table/column/row permissions on top of IAM, LF-Tags make those grants scale to large numbers of tables, and Blueprints automate common ingestion setup.

days.title: Redshift Deep Dive: RA3, Serverless, and Spectrum

concepts.heading: RA3 Nodes and Compute/Storage Separation
concepts.body: RA3 node types decouple compute from storage -- data is stored durably in a managed layer backed by S3 while compute nodes handle query processing and use high-speed local caching for frequently accessed data -- so you can scale compute up or down for performance without having to also provision more storage, and vice versa. This is a major shift from earlier dense-storage/dense-compute node types, where storage and compute scaled together whether you needed both or not.

concepts.heading: Redshift Serverless for Variable Workloads
concepts.body: Redshift Serverless automatically provisions and scales compute capacity based on query demand, billing per second of actual usage, with no cluster to size or manage. It's the preferred option when usage is intermittent or hard to predict, since a provisioned cluster sized for peak load would otherwise sit idle (and billing) most of the time.

concepts.heading: Redshift Spectrum for Querying S3 Directly
concepts.body: Redshift Spectrum lets a Redshift cluster query data sitting in S3 as external tables -- referencing the Glue Data Catalog for schema -- without first loading it into the cluster's own storage, enabling a lakehouse pattern where hot data lives in Redshift and cold/raw data stays in S3 but is still queryable via the same SQL interface. Spectrum uses separate, elastically scaled compute from your provisioned cluster for the S3-scanning portion of a query, which is billed per TB scanned similarly to Athena.

concepts.heading: Distribution Keys, Sort Keys, and WLM
concepts.body: How data is physically distributed across compute nodes (distribution key) and ordered within each node (sort key) heavily influences join and filter performance -- a poorly chosen distribution key can force expensive data redistribution across the network for every join. Workload Management (WLM) lets administrators define query queues with priorities and concurrency limits so that, for example, long analytical queries don't starve short interactive dashboard queries of resources.

examPoints: A requirement to query data sitting in S3 directly via SQL, joined against tables already in Redshift, without first loading the S3 data into the cluster, is the defining use case for Redshift Spectrum.
Intermittent or hard-to-predict usage where paying for an always-on cluster feels wasteful is the signal for Redshift Serverless over a fixed provisioned cluster.

quiz.q: A team needs to run SQL joins between data already in Redshift and large log files sitting in S3, without first loading those logs into the cluster. What should they use?
quiz.explain: Spectrum queries S3 data directly as external tables joined against native Redshift tables, without requiring a load step.

quiz.q: Usage of a Redshift data warehouse is highly intermittent, and the team doesn't want to pay for an always-on cluster. What is the best fit?
quiz.explain: Serverless bills per second of actual query usage and requires no cluster sizing, which matches intermittent, unpredictable demand better than a fixed provisioned cluster.

days.recap: RA3 separates compute from storage, Serverless removes cluster management for variable workloads, and Spectrum queries S3 data directly as part of a lakehouse pattern alongside distribution/sort keys and WLM for performance tuning.

days.title: DynamoDB from a Data Engineer's Perspective

concepts.heading: Partition Key Design and Hot Partitions
concepts.body: DynamoDB distributes items across partitions based on a hash of the partition key, so a key with low cardinality or skewed access (for example, using a single fixed value or a coarse date bucket as the key) concentrates traffic on one partition, throttling that partition even while overall table-level provisioned or on-demand capacity is sufficient. Choosing a high-cardinality key that spreads traffic evenly -- sometimes combined with a random or hashed suffix -- is the standard fix, directly analogous to avoiding hot shards in Kinesis.

concepts.heading: Global and Local Secondary Indexes
concepts.body: A Global Secondary Index (GSI) lets you query using a completely different partition and sort key than the base table's, supports eventual consistency, and can be added or removed after table creation -- useful when new access patterns emerge over time. A Local Secondary Index (LSI) keeps the same partition key as the base table but a different sort key, supports strongly consistent reads, but must be defined at table creation and cannot be added later. When an access pattern needs to query by an attribute not covered by the base table's key, a GSI is almost always the right answer since it is far more flexible than an LSI.

concepts.heading: DynamoDB Streams for Change Capture
concepts.body: DynamoDB Streams captures an ordered, near-real-time record of item-level modifications (inserts, updates, deletes) in a table, which can trigger a Lambda function or be consumed by other applications -- effectively a CDC mechanism for DynamoDB. This is commonly used to replicate changes into a data lake, maintain a materialized view in another store, or trigger downstream business logic immediately after a write.

concepts.heading: TTL for Automatic Item Expiration
concepts.body: Time to Live (TTL) automatically deletes items once a specified timestamp attribute passes, without consuming write capacity for the deletion and without requiring a separate cleanup job -- well suited to session data, temporary caches, or any dataset with a defined, short lifespan. Deletion happens in the background, typically within 48 hours of expiry rather than at the exact instant, and expired-but-not-yet-purged items can still appear briefly in scans, which is a subtle behavior worth remembering for exam scenarios.

examPoints: A requirement to propagate DynamoDB table changes to another pipeline or trigger downstream logic in near real time is the signature use case for DynamoDB Streams plus Lambda.

A new access pattern that needs a different sort order or filter attribute than the base table supports points to adding a GSI, since it's flexible and can be added after the table already exists, unlike an LSI.

quiz.q: A team needs to capture every change made to a DynamoDB table and propagate it to a downstream analytics pipeline in near real time. What should they use?
quiz.explain: DynamoDB Streams captures item-level change events directly from the table; the other options don't natively capture DynamoDB table changes.

quiz.q: A new reporting requirement needs to query a DynamoDB table using a partition key and sort key combination different from the existing table design, and it must be addable without recreating the table. What should be added?
choices: A change to the TTL setting
Only Local Secondary Indexes are possible
quiz.explain: A GSI supports a different partition/sort key combination and can be added after table creation, unlike an LSI, which must be defined at creation time.

days.recap: Hot partitions are a key-design problem solved by higher-cardinality keys; GSIs support new query patterns added after the fact; Streams provide near-real-time change capture; and TTL automates expiration of short-lived items.

days.title: The Data Store Decision Tree

concepts.heading: OLTP vs. OLAP: RDS/Aurora vs. Redshift
concepts.body: Transactional workloads with frequent small reads/writes, strong consistency needs, and normalized relational schemas belong on RDS or Aurora (OLTP), while large-scale analytical queries that aggregate across huge historical datasets belong on Redshift (OLAP), which is columnar and optimized for scanning many rows across few columns rather than fast single-row lookups. Using Redshift for transactional workloads or RDS for heavy analytical aggregation both perform poorly relative to the purpose-built alternative.

concepts.heading: Key-Value at Scale: DynamoDB
concepts.body: DynamoDB is the default answer whenever a scenario calls for single-digit-millisecond latency, key-based lookups, and automatic scaling to very high request rates, especially for access patterns known in advance (get-item-by-key rather than ad hoc analytical queries). It is a poor fit for complex multi-attribute ad hoc querying or joins, which is where a relational or analytical store is preferable.

concepts.heading: Full-Text Search and Log Analytics: OpenSearch
concepts.body: Amazon OpenSearch Service is purpose-built for full-text search, log analytics, and near-real-time dashboarding over semi-structured text data, offering inverted-index search capabilities that relational or key-value stores don't provide efficiently. It commonly ingests data via Amazon Data Firehose or Logstash-style pipelines and pairs with OpenSearch Dashboards for visualization. Scenarios mentioning searching free-text fields, ranking search relevance, or visualizing application/infrastructure logs point here rather than to Redshift or DynamoDB.

concepts.heading: Time-Series Data: Amazon Timestream
concepts.body: Amazon Timestream for InfluxDB is a managed, purpose-built time-series database (running open-source InfluxDB) designed for workloads like IoT telemetry or infrastructure metrics, where data arrives continuously tagged with a timestamp and queries typically aggregate over time windows, with single-digit-millisecond query response times for real-time analytics. The original serverless engine, Timestream for LiveAnalytics (with its in-memory and magnetic storage tiers), has been closed to new customers since 2025-06-20, and AWS recommends Timestream for InfluxDB instead. It scales far better for this specific pattern than trying to model time-series data in a general-purpose relational or NoSQL store.

concepts.heading: S3 as the Default Hub for Everything Else
concepts.body: For large volumes of semi-structured or raw data that must be retained cheaply and shared across many different analytical engines (Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR, SageMaker), S3 functions as the default data lake hub -- the place data lands first before being selectively loaded into a more specialized store like Redshift or DynamoDB for a specific access pattern.

examPoints: Classifying the described access pattern first -- single-key lookup, complex analytical aggregation, full-text search, or time-series -- narrows the correct store before you even look closely at the answer choices.

'Low-latency key-value lookup with automatic scaling' almost always means DynamoDB, while 'complex SQL joins across large historical datasets' almost always means Redshift -- these two phrasings are the most frequently tested pair in this domain.

quiz.q: An application needs to full-text search application logs and visualize them on a dashboard. Which service is best suited?
quiz.explain: OpenSearch is purpose-built for full-text search and log analytics with dashboarding, unlike DynamoDB or Redshift.

quiz.q: Millions of IoT sensor readings must be ingested and analyzed per second, each tagged with a precise timestamp, with queries typically aggregating over recent time windows. Which store is the best fit?
quiz.explain: Timestream for InfluxDB is purpose-built for high-throughput time-series ingestion and time-windowed analytics, unlike a general-purpose relational database.

days.recap: Classify the access pattern first: OLTP goes to RDS/Aurora, OLAP to Redshift, low-latency key-value to DynamoDB, full-text search to OpenSearch, time-series to Timestream for InfluxDB, and raw shared data to S3.

days.title: Data Modeling and Schema Evolution

concepts.heading: Star Schema for Analytical Modeling
concepts.body: A star schema organizes data around a central fact table (measurable events, like sales transactions) surrounded by denormalized dimension tables (like customer, product, and date), which simplifies analytical queries into straightforward joins from the fact table out to a handful of dimensions rather than many-level joins through a normalized schema. A snowflake schema is a variant that further normalizes dimension tables into sub-dimensions, trading some query simplicity for reduced redundancy.

concepts.heading: Normalization vs. Denormalization Trade-offs
concepts.body: Normalized schemas minimize data redundancy and optimize for consistent, efficient writes, which suits transactional (OLTP) systems, while denormalized schemas duplicate some data to minimize the number of joins needed at query time, which suits analytical (OLAP) read-heavy workloads. A data engineer moving data from an OLTP source into an OLAP warehouse typically denormalizes deliberately during the transformation step, rather than preserving the source's normalized structure.

concepts.heading: Schema Versioning in the Glue Data Catalog
concepts.body: The Glue Data Catalog retains a version history of a table's schema, so when a source adds a column or changes a data type, the catalog can track that evolution while downstream consumers determine whether the new schema is backward compatible. Handling schema drift gracefully -- rather than having a pipeline break the moment an upstream schema changes -- depends on catalog versioning combined with formats like Avro or Iceberg that natively support compatible schema evolution.

concepts.heading: Hot-Warm-Cold Data Lifecycle Tiers
concepts.body: Data lifecycle management maps logical tiers -- hot (frequently accessed, needs the fastest retrieval), warm (accessed occasionally), and cold (rarely accessed, retained for compliance or historical analysis) -- onto concrete implementation choices like S3 storage class transitions and partition-based access patterns, so that storage cost scales down automatically as data ages and becomes less relevant to day-to-day queries.

examPoints: A question about designing a schema for an analytical data warehouse, where query simplicity matters more than write efficiency, almost always points to a star schema as the standard answer.

A source system whose schema changes frequently, where downstream compatibility must be maintained, points to schema-evolution-friendly formats (Avro/Iceberg) plus Glue Data Catalog version tracking, rather than a rigid fixed-schema format like plain CSV.

quiz.q: What is the standard schema design pattern for simplifying queries in an analytical data warehouse?
choices: A single fully denormalized table with no keys at all
quiz.explain: A star schema (fact plus dimension tables) is the standard pattern for simplifying analytical queries, unlike highly normalized 3NF designs meant for OLTP.

quiz.q: A source system's schema changes frequently, and downstream consumers need to track those changes while maintaining backward compatibility. What should the team rely on?
choices: A fixed CSV format with no changes allowed
Glue Data Catalog schema versioning combined with a schema-evolution-friendly format
Dropping and recreating the table on every change
quiz.explain: Catalog versioning tracks schema changes over time, and formats like Avro/Iceberg are explicitly designed to evolve schemas compatibly.

days.recap: Star schemas are the analytical modeling standard, normalization vs. denormalization trades write efficiency for read simplicity, and Glue Data Catalog versioning plus evolution-friendly formats handle schema drift.

days.title: Domain 2 Review: Data Store Management

concepts.heading: The Domain 2 Service Map
concepts.body: Domain 2 spans the S3 storage-class and lifecycle layer, Lake Formation governance on top of the lake, Redshift for large-scale SQL analytics, DynamoDB for low-latency key-value access, and the broader decision tree for choosing among purpose-built stores based on access pattern. As with Domain 1, the exam rewards being able to place a described requirement into this map quickly rather than recalling facts about each service in isolation.

concepts.heading: Athena vs. Redshift Spectrum: A Frequent Head-to-Head
concepts.body: Both Athena and Redshift Spectrum query data sitting in S3 directly using SQL and both reference the Glue Data Catalog for schema, but Athena is fully serverless and billed per query with no cluster required at all, while Spectrum uses the compute of an existing Redshift cluster to scan S3 data alongside native Redshift tables. If a scenario has no existing Redshift cluster, Athena is the simpler and more cost-appropriate choice; if a cluster is already running and needs to join S3 data with existing warehouse tables, Spectrum is a better fit.

concepts.heading: Governance and Storage Working Together
concepts.body: Lake Formation, S3 storage classes/lifecycle, and Redshift/DynamoDB access patterns are frequently combined in scenario questions -- for example, an S3-based lake with Lake Formation governance feeding curated data into Redshift for BI reporting, with Lifecycle rules aging out the rawest data automatically. Reviewing how these pieces connect end-to-end, rather than as isolated topics, mirrors how the exam frequently frames multi-step architecture questions that span ingestion, storage, and access control in a single scenario.

concepts.heading: Modeling and Format Choices, Revisited
concepts.body: Star schemas, normalization trade-offs, and schema-evolution-friendly formats from Day 15 round out Domain 2's coverage: knowing how to store data (S3/Redshift/DynamoDB), how to govern it (Lake Formation), and how to model it (star schema, versioned schema) together gives a complete picture of 'managing a data store' as the exam intends the phrase, rather than treating storage and modeling as unrelated topics.

examPoints: Domain 2 is worth 26% of the exam -- S3 storage/lifecycle, Redshift, DynamoDB, and Lake Formation alone cover the large majority of its scenario questions.

When deciding between Athena and Redshift Spectrum, the presence or absence of an already-running Redshift cluster is usually the deciding factor in the question, more than any subtle performance difference.

quiz.q: A team has no existing Redshift cluster and wants to run ad hoc SQL queries against data sitting in S3 in a serverless way. What should they use?
quiz.explain: Athena queries S3 directly with no cluster required, unlike Spectrum, which needs an existing Redshift cluster to provide its compute.

quiz.q: Which service provides table-, column-, and row-level access control across a data lake, layered on top of IAM?
quiz.explain: Lake Formation adds fine-grained data lake permissions beyond what IAM alone can express.

days.recap: Domain 2 review complete: if you can explain S3 tiering, Lake Formation governance, Redshift, and DynamoDB's roles in one sentence each, you're ready for Domain 3.

days.title: Operationalizing Pipelines: Reruns and Backfills

concepts.heading: CI/CD for Data Pipeline Code
concepts.body: CodePipeline and CodeBuild together automate testing and deployment of pipeline code -- Glue job scripts, Lambda functions, Step Functions definitions -- so changes go through automated validation before reaching production rather than being deployed manually. This reduces the risk of a bad change silently breaking a production pipeline and gives you an audit trail of what changed and when.

concepts.heading: Backfilling Historical Data
concepts.body: A backfill reprocesses historical data, typically because a bug in transformation logic was fixed or a new column needs to be computed retroactively; the standard mechanism is to reset the Job Bookmark (or bypass it) and explicitly pass a date range as a job parameter so the job knows exactly which historical partitions to reprocess, rather than relying on bookmark state meant for incremental forward processing.

concepts.heading: Partition-Level Reruns vs. Full Reruns
concepts.body: When only specific partitions failed (for example, one day's worth of data out of a year), reprocessing just those partitions is far cheaper and faster than rerunning the entire pipeline from scratch, but it requires the job to be idempotent -- safely overwriting or upserting the same partition without producing duplicates if run twice. Designing jobs this way from the start makes partial reruns and backfills routine operations rather than risky, ad hoc procedures.

concepts.heading: Blue/Green and Canary Deployments for Pipeline Changes
concepts.body: Rolling out pipeline code changes gradually -- for example, running the new version alongside the old (blue/green) or on a small subset of traffic first (canary) -- limits the blast radius if a change introduces a regression, compared to deploying directly to 100% of production traffic. This is the same deployment-risk-reduction principle used for application code, applied to data pipelines.

examPoints: A requirement to reprocess a specific historical date range after fixing a transformation bug is the standard trigger for resetting a Job Bookmark and passing an explicit date-range parameter, rather than letting bookmark state handle it automatically.

'Retry only the failed step, not the whole pipeline' maps directly to Step Functions' Retry and Catch configuration on individual states, rather than restarting the entire state machine from the beginning.

quiz.q: A transformation bug affecting the last three months of processed data has just been fixed, and that data must be reprocessed with the corrected logic. What is the standard approach?
choices: Build an entirely new job from scratch
Reset the Job Bookmark and rerun with an explicit date-range parameter for the affected period
Delete and recreate the S3 bucket
quiz.explain: Resetting the bookmark and specifying the date range explicitly is the standard backfill pattern; bookmarks alone are designed for incremental forward processing, not deliberate backfills.

quiz.q: What deployment strategy reduces risk when rolling out a change to pipeline code?
choices: A CI/CD pipeline with automated testing and staged rollout
Manually replace files with no testing
Replace everything at once with no backup
quiz.explain: Automated testing plus staged (blue/green or canary) rollout limits the blast radius of a bad change compared to an untested, all-at-once deployment.

days.recap: Backfills reset Job Bookmarks with explicit date parameters, reruns should target only failed partitions and require idempotent jobs, and CI/CD with staged rollout manages deployment risk.

days.title: Monitoring: CloudWatch, CloudTrail, and X-Ray

concepts.heading: CloudWatch Metrics and Alarms
concepts.body: CloudWatch collects per-service operational metrics -- Glue DPU utilization and job run duration, Kinesis IteratorAge, DynamoDB throttled requests, and many others -- and lets you set alarms that trigger when a metric crosses a threshold, typically notifying an SNS topic so a team is alerted before a small issue becomes a major outage. Knowing which metric to watch for which service is a frequently tested, very concrete piece of exam knowledge.

concepts.heading: IteratorAge as a Streaming Lag Indicator
concepts.body: The Kinesis metric GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds measures how far behind a consumer is relative to the latest record written to the stream; a steadily increasing IteratorAge means the consumer cannot keep up with the producer's write rate, indicating the consumer needs more parallelism (more shards, more Lambda concurrency, or Enhanced Fan-Out) rather than a stream-capacity problem on the write side.

concepts.heading: CloudTrail for API Audit Logging
concepts.body: CloudTrail records every API call made against your AWS account -- who made it, when, from where, and what the request/response looked like -- which is the tool to reach for whenever a scenario asks 'who changed this bucket policy' or 'was this IAM role used to access this resource', as opposed to operational metrics, which CloudTrail does not provide.

concepts.heading: X-Ray for Distributed Request Tracing
concepts.body: AWS X-Ray traces a single request as it flows through multiple services (for example, API Gateway to Lambda to DynamoDB), visualizing exactly where latency accumulates across that chain as a service map with per-segment timing -- a capability neither CloudWatch metrics nor CloudTrail logs provide on their own, since both operate per-service rather than per-request-across-services. It's most valuable when a pipeline's overall latency is high but it's unclear which specific downstream call is responsible.

examPoints: A question about detecting streaming pipeline lag will usually reference IteratorAge for Kinesis; a question about batch pipeline health will more likely reference Glue job duration or DPU metrics -- know both.
'Who changed this configuration and when' is always a CloudTrail question, never a CloudWatch or X-Ray question, since only CloudTrail records API-level audit history.

quiz.q: Which metric indicates whether a Kinesis Data Streams consumer is falling behind the rate at which producers are writing records?
quiz.explain: A rising IteratorAge means the consumer is processing records that are increasingly old relative to the stream's latest write, indicating consumer lag.

quiz.q: A security team needs to determine exactly who changed a specific IAM policy and when. What should they consult?
quiz.explain: CloudTrail records the audit history of every API call, including who made a change and when, which CloudWatch and X-Ray do not provide.

days.recap: IteratorAge signals Kinesis consumer lag, CloudTrail provides API-level audit history, X-Ray traces latency across a distributed request chain, and CloudWatch alarms plus SNS deliver proactive notification.

days.title: Query and Visualization: Athena and QuickSight

concepts.heading: Athena Workgroups for Cost and Access Isolation
concepts.body: Athena workgroups let you segregate queries by team or project, each with its own query result location, per-query or per-workgroup data-scanned budget limits, and separate IAM permissions, preventing one team's runaway query from silently consuming another's cost budget and giving finance visibility into per-team query spend. Combined with per-workgroup CloudWatch metrics, workgroups also make it straightforward to alert when a team approaches its configured data-scanned limit before it is actually exceeded.

concepts.heading: CTAS for Materializing Optimized Query Results
concepts.body: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) runs a query and persists its result as a brand-new table, commonly used to convert a raw CSV/JSON table into a partitioned Parquet table in one step, or to pre-aggregate a frequently-run expensive query into a smaller, faster-to-query result table. This is a standard technique for optimizing recurring analytical queries without changing the underlying source data.

concepts.heading: Partition Projection for Large Partition Counts
concepts.body: Partition projection lets Athena compute a table's partitions algorithmically from a defined rule (for example, a date range and format) at query time, instead of requiring every partition to be registered in the Glue Data Catalog ahead of time. This avoids the slow crawler runs and catalog sync overhead that come with tables having tens of thousands of partitions, since Athena simply calculates which S3 prefixes to look at directly from the projection rule.

concepts.heading: QuickSight and the SPICE In-Memory Engine
concepts.body: Amazon QuickSight is a serverless BI and visualization service, and its SPICE engine caches a copy of query results in memory so that dashboards render quickly for many concurrent viewers without re-querying the underlying data source on every page load. SPICE datasets need to be refreshed on a schedule to reflect new source data, which is a trade-off between dashboard performance and data freshness that a scenario question may probe.

examPoints: A table with tens of thousands of partitions causing slow Glue Catalog sync or crawler runs is the classic signal for partition projection, which computes partitions algorithmically instead of registering each one.

'Convert query results into a new, optimized table' -- especially converting row-based to columnar format -- describes CTAS, distinct from a plain INSERT INTO, which appends to an existing table rather than creating a new optimized one.

quiz.q: A table has grown to tens of thousands of partitions, and Glue Catalog synchronization has become slow. What should be used to improve this?
quiz.explain: Partition projection computes partitions from a rule at query time rather than registering each one in the catalog, removing the sync bottleneck entirely.

quiz.q: A team wants to persist the result of an expensive Athena query as a new, compressed, columnar table for faster future queries. What should they use?
quiz.explain: CTAS materializes a query's result as a new table, commonly used to switch to an optimized format like Parquet in the same step.

days.recap: Athena workgroups isolate cost and access per team, CTAS materializes optimized result tables, partition projection scales past large partition counts, and QuickSight's SPICE engine caches data for fast dashboards.

days.title: Data Quality with AWS Glue Data Quality

concepts.heading: Declarative Rules with DQDL
concepts.body: AWS Glue Data Quality lets you define rules in the Data Quality Definition Language (DQDL) -- for example, asserting that a column's completeness is above 95%, that values fall within an expected range, or that a column is unique -- and evaluates a dataset against those rules automatically as part of a pipeline, producing a pass/fail score rather than requiring custom validation code written by hand.

concepts.heading: Profiling Before Defining Rules
concepts.body: Before writing quality rules, it's standard practice to first profile the data (often with Glue DataBrew) to understand actual distributions, missing-value rates, and outliers, so the rules you define reflect the data's real characteristics rather than guesses. Skipping profiling tends to produce either rules that are too loose to catch real problems or too strict and generate constant false-positive failures.

concepts.heading: Schema Drift Detection
concepts.body: Schema drift occurs when an upstream source changes its structure -- adding, removing, or renaming a column, or changing a data type -- without warning, which can silently break downstream jobs that assume a fixed schema. Detecting drift typically relies on scheduled crawler runs combined with alerting when the inferred schema differs from the previously cataloged one, so the team can react before it causes silent data corruption rather than an outright job failure.

concepts.heading: Fail vs. Quarantine Policies
concepts.body: When quality checks fail, a pipeline can either fail the entire run (Fail) to prevent any bad data from propagating, or route only the failing records to a separate quarantine location while allowing the rest of the good data to continue processing (Quarantine). The choice depends on whether partial, mostly-correct data delivered on time is more valuable to downstream consumers than delaying everything until the bad records are fixed -- a trade-off the exam expects you to reason through rather than assume one answer is always correct.

examPoints: A requirement to automatically and declaratively verify that column values fall within an expected range or format is the Glue Data Quality / DQDL use case, not a custom Lambda validation function.
'Isolate only the failing records while letting the rest of the pipeline continue' describes a Quarantine policy specifically, as distinct from a Fail policy, which stops the entire pipeline run.

quiz.q: A team wants to declaratively verify that a numeric column's values fall within an expected range as part of an automated pipeline. What should they use?
quiz.explain: Glue Data Quality with DQDL defines and enforces declarative data quality rules like range checks; the other services address security/compliance, not data quality.

quiz.q: A pipeline should isolate records that fail quality checks into a separate location while continuing to process the remaining valid records. What policy should be applied?
choices: A Quarantine policy for failing records
Ignore the failures and log only
quiz.explain: A Quarantine policy separates only the failing records, allowing the pipeline to continue processing the valid majority of the data.

days.recap: DQDL defines declarative quality rules, profiling should come before rule design, schema drift needs proactive detection, and Quarantine policies isolate bad records while Fail policies stop the whole run.

days.title: Troubleshooting Scenarios: A Field Guide

concepts.heading: Glue Job Out-of-Memory Failures
concepts.body: A Glue Spark job failing with out-of-memory errors during a large join is usually caused by data skew (a small number of keys with disproportionately many rows) rather than simply insufficient total capacity; the standard remediation order is to first diagnose and address skew (via salting or repartitioning) and only then increase Worker Type or worker count if skew alone doesn't explain the failure.

concepts.heading: Kinesis Hot Shards and Throttling
concepts.body: Kinesis throttling concentrated on specific shards points back to a partition-key design issue (as covered on Day 2), while a producer seeing widespread PutRecord failures across all shards more likely indicates the stream genuinely needs more total shard capacity. Producers should always implement retry with exponential backoff regardless of the root cause, since transient throttling is expected behavior under load.

concepts.heading: Redshift WLM Queue Bottlenecks
concepts.body: When queries pile up waiting in a Workload Management (WLM) queue during peak periods, Concurrency Scaling can automatically add temporary, transient compute capacity to absorb the burst of additional queries without a manual cluster resize, and it's specifically designed for short-term spikes rather than sustained capacity increases, for which resizing the cluster itself would be more appropriate.

concepts.heading: DMS Replication Lag
